name: Agnihotra (daily fire-offering)
method_summary: Twice daily, at sunrise and sunset, the householder who has established the sacred fires offers milk into the āhavanīya fire. The Brāhmaṇas explain it as healing the junction of day and night in Prajāpati (ŚB 1.6.3.36), as an offering of 'truth in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1), as a cycle of the oblations through the worlds into man and woman (ŚB 11.6.2), and as protection from retribution in the other world (ŚB 11.6.1).
stage: householder who has set up the fires (āhitāgni)

equivalents.note: ChU 5.24 calls the breath-offering the true Agnihotra

name: Agnyādheya (establishing the sacred fires)
method_summary: The rite by which a householder sets up his three Śrauta fires; the Brāhmaṇas fix its times by season and lunar mansion (the Kṛttikās, ŚB 2.1.2.3).

name: New- and full-moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa)
method_summary: The fortnightly Śrauta offerings of cakes and other oblations, entered with a vow of truth (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5), which heal the joints of the year-Prajāpati at the moon's phases (ŚB 1.6.3.36).

name: Agnicayana (building the fire-altar)
method_summary: The year-long construction of a great brick altar in five layers, typically in the form of a bird, within a Soma sacrifice; understood as rebuilding Prajāpati and constructing an immortal self (ŚB 6–10); the Śulbasūtras give its geometry. Its secret doctrine interiorizes it as fires built of mind and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3).

name: Pravargya (the hot-milk rite)
method_summary: A rite within the Soma sacrifice in which milk is heated in a clay pot (mahāvīra) until it glows; explained as restoring the head of the sacrifice cut off from Makha/Viṣṇu (ŚB 14.1–3; TA 4–5); secret, taught apart.

warnings.text: Treated as a dangerous, secret rite to be learned apart (in the Āraṇyaka) from a qualified teacher.

name: Dīkṣā (consecration for sacrifice)
method_summary: Before a Soma sacrifice the sacrificer is consecrated in a hut with vows of fasting and restraint; the priests make him an embryo again (AB 1.3); he is born anew at the final bath.

name: Rājasūya (royal consecration)
method_summary: The Śrauta consecration of a king, during which the story of Śunaḥśepa is recited (AB 7.13–18).

name: Vrātyastoma (rites for admitting Vrātyas)
method_summary: Soma rites by which groups living outside the sacrificial order are made fit to sacrifice (PB 17.1–4).

name: Piṇḍapitṛyajña (monthly offering of rice-balls to the fathers)
method_summary: The Śrauta new-moon offering of rice-balls to the three nearest ancestors, performed with the sacred cord over the right shoulder, since the fathers receive food monthly (ŚB 2.4.2).

name: Prāṇāgnihotra (offering food into the breaths)
method_summary: At each meal the eater sips water ('immortal under-layer'), offers the first five morsels with 'svāhā' to prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna and samāna, meditating that each breath, sense, deity and region is satisfied, and ends with water ('immortal covering'); eating is thus an Agnihotra offered in the self (ChU 5.19–24; TA 10.69–70).
signs_of_progress: 'his evils are burned up like a reed-tuft in fire' (ChU 5.24.3)

warnings.text: Offered without knowing its meaning, the Agnihotra is 'like pouring the offering on ashes' (ChU 5.24.1).

name: Pratardana's inner Agnihotra (saṃyamana)
method_summary: Knowing that while speaking one offers breath into speech and while breathing offers speech into breath, one treats these as two endless oblations offered continuously, waking and sleeping (KU 2.5 = ŚĀ 4.5).

name: Śāṇḍilya-vidyā (meditation on the self made of mind)
method_summary: Resolving that one becomes at death what one's resolve is, one meditates on the self as made of mind, with breath for body, of the form of light, small as a grain within and greater than all worlds, and resolves to attain it on departing (ŚB 10.6.3; ChU 3.14).

name: Svādhyāya (daily Vedic self-study; brahmayajña)
method_summary: Daily recitation of one's Veda, at least a portion, as the sacrifice to Brahman (ŚB 11.5.6.3; TA 2.10); it brings concentration, independence, sound sleep and delight in the one thing (ŚB 11.5.7.1).

warnings.text: Recitation is suspended on the prescribed non-study occasions (anadhyāya).

name: The Vedic recitations (pāṭha): continuous, word-by-word, step and the eight modified ones
method_summary: The pupil learns the text orally from the teacher in the continuous form (saṃhitā), word by word (pada), in overlapping pairs (krama) and in the elaborate 'modified' patterns (jaṭā, ghana and others), with exact accent and quantity, pronouncing each sound 'as a tigress carries her cubs' (PŚ 25) and avoiding the six faults of reciters (PŚ 32).

warnings.text: A mantra faulty in accent or sound harms the sacrificer (PŚ 52).
Reciting without understanding is 'dry fuel without fire' (Nirukta 1.18).

name: Recitation of the Sāvitrī (Gāyatrī)
method_summary: Recitation of the Sāvitrī verse preceded by Oṃ and the three utterances, especially at the twilights (MDh 2.76–78; YS 1.22–25).

name: Japa — audible, whispered, mental
method_summary: Repetition of a mantra, which surpasses ritual sacrifice tenfold when audible, a hundredfold when whispered and a thousandfold when mental; by japa alone a brāhmaṇa can reach perfection (MDh 2.85–87).

name: Sandhyā (twilight worship)
method_summary: At dawn and dusk: sipping and bathing, sprinkling with the water-verses, breath-control with the Gāyatrī, offering water to the sun (which scatters the Mandeha demons, TA 2.2), and reciting the Sāvitrī standing till sunrise or sitting till the stars appear (YS 1.22–25); the sun is meditated on as Brahman.

name: Breath-control with Oṃ, the utterances and the Gāyatrī
method_summary: Breath-control performed while mentally reciting the Gāyatrī with its 'head', preceded by the utterances and with Oṃ, as part of the twilight worship and as the renouncer's austerity; it burns away the faults of the senses (MDh 6.70–72; YS 1.23; VDh 10.5).
notes: No retention counts or durations are recorded here.

name: Aghamarṣaṇa (sin-effacing recitation)
method_summary: Recitation of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn (RV 10.190), traditionally while immersed in water, which removes sin as the horse-sacrifice does (MDh 11.261; GDh 19.12).

name: The five great daily sacrifices
method_summary: Each day the householder studies/teaches the Veda (to Brahman), offers water to the ancestors, an oblation into fire to the gods, food-offerings (bali) to beings and hospitality to guests (to men) (ŚB 11.5.6.1–3; TA 2.10; MDh 3.68–70).

name: The householder's daily round (āhnika)
method_summary: Waking at the hour of Brahmā to reflect on dharma, artha, bodily strain and the meaning of the Veda (MDh 4.92), purification, twilight worship, study, the five great sacrifices, work and meals with the breath-offerings, and evening worship.

name: Vedic studentship (brahmacarya), temporary or lifelong
method_summary: Living in the teacher's house after initiation: begging, bringing fuel, tending the fire, serving the teacher, chastity and study; the lifelong (naiṣṭhika) student serves the teacher until death (MDh 2; ŚB 11.3.3).
duration: 12 years per Veda or until mastered; or lifelong

name: Renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in the Dharmaśāstra
method_summary: After the Prājāpatya sacrifice with all possessions given away, the renouncer deposits the fires in himself and goes forth giving safety to all beings; he lives alone, without fire or house, begging once a day, purifying step, water, speech and act, delighting in the self, practising breath-control and meditation, neither welcoming death nor life (MDh 6.33–85); he must not renounce the Veda (VDh 10.4).
stage: after the debts are paid (or, in other views, from any stage)

warnings.text: Seeking liberation without paying the three debts leads downward (MDh 6.35–37).

name: The great departure (mahāprasthāna)
method_summary: Summary only: a forest-hermit may set out towards the north-east, living on water and air, intent on yoga, until the body falls (MDh 6.31).

warnings.text: Later Dharmaśāstra authorities list the great departure among practices forbidden in the Kali age (kalivarjya).

notes: Restricted: recorded as the text states it; no instructions.

name: Garbhādhāna (rite for conception)
method_summary: The rite performed by the husband at the proper time for conception, first of the bodily sacraments (MDh 2.26–27; YS 1.11).

name: Puṃsavana (rite for a male child)
method_summary: A rite in the third month of pregnancy, before the embryo 'moves', for a male child.

name: Sīmantonnayana (parting of the hair)
method_summary: A rite in the later months of pregnancy in which the husband parts the wife's hair for her and the child's protection.

name: Jātakarma (birth rite)
method_summary: At birth, before the cord is cut, the father gives the child honey and ghee, whispers 'speech' in its ear and wishes it long life and intelligence.

name: Nāmakaraṇa (naming)
method_summary: Naming the child on the tenth or twelfth day, with names auspicious and suited to the class.

name: Niṣkramaṇa (first outing)
method_summary: Taking the child out to see the sun in the fourth month.

name: Annaprāśana (first solid food)
method_summary: Feeding the child its first solid food in the sixth month.

name: Cūḍākaraṇa (tonsure)
method_summary: Shaving the child's head, leaving the tuft, in the first or third year (MDh 2.35).

name: Karṇavedha (ear-piercing)
method_summary: Piercing the child's ears, a later addition to the lists.

name: Vidyārambha (beginning of letters)
method_summary: Beginning the learning of the alphabet, a later addition to the lists.

name: Keśānta / Godāna (first shave)
method_summary: The first shaving of the beard at about sixteen, with a gift of a cow.

name: Samāvartana (return home, final bath)
method_summary: The ceremonial bath (snāna) ending studentship, after which the graduate (snātaka) may marry; he keeps the snātaka rules (MDh 4).

name: Upanayana (initiation into Vedic study)
method_summary: The boy asks to become a student; the teacher takes his hand, invests him with girdle (of muñja grass for a brāhmaṇa), staff, deerskin and (later) sacred thread, and teaches him the Sāvitrī; he is now 'twice-born' with the Sāvitrī as mother and teacher as father. Due at eight, eleven or twelve years for the three classes (ŚB 11.5.4; ĀśGS 1.19–22; MDh 2.36–40; 2.169–171).

name: Vivāha (marriage)
method_summary: The householder's sacrament, following regional and village custom (ĀśGS 1.7.1): the taking of the bride's hand, circling the fire, stepping on the stone, the seven steps, and establishing the domestic fire; eight forms of marriage are recognized (MDh 3.21).

name: Antyeṣṭi (funeral rites)
method_summary: The dying āhitāgni goes out with his fires; the body is washed, carried to the cremation ground and burned (an āhitāgni with his sacred fires and ritual implements placed on his limbs), with the Yama hymn and funeral mantras; infants under two are buried; the relatives bathe and offer water, observe ten days' impurity, collect the bones, and later a funeral mound may be built (ĀśGS 4.1–6; YS 3.1–2; MDh 5.59–68; ŚB 12.5.2; 13.8; TA 6).

name: Udakakarma (water-offerings for the dead)
method_summary: Relatives offer water (with sesame) to the deceased after the cremation and during the days of impurity; not done for infants under two (YS 3.1).

name: Asthisañcayana (collecting the bones)
method_summary: On a fixed day after cremation the bones are gathered into an urn, later buried or deposited in water (ĀśGS 4.5).

name: Observance of death-impurity
method_summary: For ten days (or by class) the sapiṇḍa relatives refrain from rites, study, certain foods and contact, ending with purificatory bathing (MDh 5.59–83).

name: Śrāddha (offering to the ancestors)
method_summary: Qualified brāhmaṇas are invited and fed as the ancestors' representatives, rice-balls (piṇḍa) are offered to the father, grandfather and great-grandfather, and water and sesame given; performed monthly at the new moon and on death-anniversaries and other occasions (MDh 3.122–286).

name: Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa (uniting the dead with the ancestors)
method_summary: The rite that merges the piṇḍa of the newly dead with those of his three forefathers, making the preta a pitṛ (on the twelfth day or at the end of the first year, by different authorities).

name: Expiation by confession, remorse, austerity and recitation
method_summary: The sinner declares his deed, repents, resolves not to repeat it, performs austerity and Vedic recitation (and gives gifts in distress); as the mind condemns the deed, so the body is freed from it (MDh 11.227–232).

name: Kṛcchra penances
method_summary: Summary only: graded expiatory penances regulating food and water over a set period (Prājāpatya, Sāṃtapana, Atikṛcchra, Taptakṛcchra, Parāka) (MDh 11.211–215).

warnings.text: Penances are to be undertaken according to one's capacity and under the direction of learned authorities; the digests allow substitutes for those unable to perform them.

notes: Restricted (prolonged fasting): no quantities or durations recorded. The warning is paraphrased at chapter level (moderate).

name: Cāndrāyaṇa (lunar penance)
method_summary: Summary only: an expiatory fast in which food follows the waning and waxing of the moon over a month (MDh 11.216).

warnings.text: To be performed only as prescribed expiation, with the observances and self-control the texts require.
